title: Aggregate Department Payroll via Derived Table
description_markdown: From a subquery in the FROM clause that calculates `dept_id` and `AVG(salary) AS avg_salary` for each department in `employees`, select `dept_id` and `ROUND(avg_salary, 2) AS rounded_avg` where `avg_salary >= 130000`. Exclude NULL `dept_id`. Order by `dept_id`.
starter_query:
-- Derived table in FROM
SELECT dept_id, ROUND(avg_salary, 2) AS rounded_avg
FROM (
  SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
  FROM employees ...
) dept_stats ...
solution_query: SELECT dept_id, ROUND(avg_salary, 2) AS rounded_avg FROM (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) dept_stats WHERE avg_salary >= 130000 ORDER BY dept_id ASC;
solution_explanation: The subquery inside FROM defines an inline derived table (`dept_stats`) with an alias that the outer query queries and filters.
hints: Every derived table in the FROM clause must have an alias (e.g. `AS dept_stats`).
Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.

Query: SELECT dept_id, ROUND(avg_salary, 2) AS rounded_avg FROM (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) dept_stats WHERE avg_salary >= 130000 ORDER BY dept_id ASC;

title: Count Customers by Number of Orders Placed
description_markdown: Using a derived table that counts orders per customer (`customer_id` and `COUNT(*) AS order_count` from `orders`), count how many customers fall into each `order_count` tier. Return `order_count` and `COUNT(*) AS total_customers`. Group by `order_count`. Order by `order_count` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Aggregate over an aggregate using derived table
SELECT ...
solution_query: SELECT order_count, COUNT(*) AS total_customers FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) user_orders GROUP BY order_count ORDER BY order_count ASC;
solution_explanation: Solves the multi-stage aggregation pattern (aggregating the count of an aggregate).
hints: Inner query: `SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id`.
Outer query: `SELECT order_count, COUNT(*) AS total_customers FROM (...) user_orders GROUP BY order_count`.
Query: SELECT order_count, COUNT(*) AS total_customers FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) user_orders GROUP BY order_count ORDER BY order_count ASC;

title: Aggregate Order Items with Stock Inventory
description_markdown: From a derived table calculating total units sold (`product_id`, `SUM(quantity) AS units_sold` from `order_items`), join with `products` on `product_id`. Return `p.product_name`, `sub.units_sold`, and `p.stock_quantity`. Order by `sub.units_sold` DESC, `p.product_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Join derived table with products
SELECT ...
solution_query: SELECT p.product_name, sub.units_sold, p.stock_quantity FROM (SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units_sold FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id) sub JOIN products p ON sub.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY sub.units_sold DESC, p.product_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Pre-aggregates line items in an inline subquery before joining to the product catalog.
hints: Join the derived subquery with `products p` on `sub.product_id = p.product_id`.
Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.

Query: SELECT p.product_name, sub.units_sold, p.stock_quantity FROM (SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units_sold FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id) sub JOIN products p ON sub.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY sub.units_sold DESC, p.product_id ASC;

title: Filter Departments by Staff Headcount via Derived Table
description_markdown: From a derived table in the FROM clause that calculates `dept_id` and `COUNT(*) AS emp_count` for each department in `employees` (excluding NULL `dept_id`), select `dept_id` and `emp_count` where `emp_count >= 3`. Order by `emp_count` DESC, `dept_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Derived table in FROM clause
SELECT dept_id, emp_count
FROM (
  SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY dept_id
) dept_counts
WHERE emp_count >= 3
ORDER BY emp_count DESC, dept_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT dept_id, emp_count FROM (SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) dept_counts WHERE emp_count >= 3 ORDER BY emp_count DESC, dept_id ASC;
solution_explanation: The derived table `dept_counts` pre-aggregates employee headcounts per department before the outer query filters and sorts the resulting relation.
common_mistakes: Omitting the mandatory alias for the subquery in the FROM clause.
interview_tip: Every derived table in the FROM clause must be assigned an alias in standard SQL and MySQL.
hints: Aggregate in the FROM subquery: `SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id`.
Alias the subquery as `dept_counts` and filter with `WHERE emp_count >= 3`.

Query: SELECT dept_id, emp_count FROM (SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) dept_counts WHERE emp_count >= 3 ORDER BY emp_count DESC, dept_id ASC;

title: Category Pricing Metrics via Derived Table
description_markdown: From a derived table in the FROM clause calculating `category_id`, `ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price`, and `COUNT(*) AS item_count` grouped by `category_id`, select `category_id`, `avg_price`, and `item_count` where `avg_price > 100.00`. Order by `category_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Derived table calculating category price metrics
SELECT category_id, avg_price, item_count
FROM (
  SELECT category_id, ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price, COUNT(*) AS item_count
  FROM products
  GROUP BY category_id
) cat_summary
WHERE avg_price > 100.00
ORDER BY category_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT category_id, avg_price, item_count FROM (SELECT category_id, ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price, COUNT(*) AS item_count FROM products GROUP BY category_id) cat_summary WHERE avg_price > 100.00 ORDER BY category_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Derived tables allow you to refer to aggregate calculation results by their column alias in the outer WHERE clause, avoiding repeated expressions.
common_mistakes: Trying to use the column alias in the inner WHERE clause.
interview_tip: Derived tables eliminate the restriction of having to use HAVING by transforming aggregates into queryable columns.
hints: Compute `ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price` in the inner query.
Filter `avg_price > 100.00` in the outer query.

Query: SELECT category_id, avg_price, item_count FROM (SELECT category_id, ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price, COUNT(*) AS item_count FROM products GROUP BY category_id) cat_summary WHERE avg_price > 100.00 ORDER BY category_id ASC;

title: Count Students per Academic Tier via Inline Categorization
description_markdown: Using a derived table in the FROM clause that assigns each student to an academic tier (`CASE WHEN gpa >= 3.5 THEN 'Honor Roll' WHEN gpa >= 3.0 THEN 'Good Standing' ELSE 'Academic Probation' END AS tier`), count how many students fall into each tier. Return `tier` and `COUNT(*) AS student_count`. Order by `student_count` DESC, `tier` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Derived table for student tier distribution
SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS student_count
FROM (
  SELECT student_id, CASE ... END AS tier
  FROM students
) student_tiers
GROUP BY tier
ORDER BY student_count DESC, tier ASC;
solution_query: SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS student_count FROM (SELECT student_id, CASE WHEN gpa >= 3.5 THEN 'Honor Roll' WHEN gpa >= 3.0 THEN 'Good Standing' ELSE 'Academic Probation' END AS tier FROM students) student_tiers GROUP BY tier ORDER BY student_count DESC, tier ASC;
solution_explanation: Derives a categorized column `tier` via a CASE expression inside a subquery, then groups by this computed label in the outer query.
common_mistakes: Duplicating the entire CASE expression in the GROUP BY without a derived table.
interview_tip: Derived tables are the cleanest way to perform bucketing/segmentation followed by aggregation.
hints: Use CASE inside the subquery to produce the `tier` column.
Group by `tier` in the outer query.

Query: SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS student_count FROM (SELECT student_id, CASE WHEN gpa >= 3.5 THEN 'Honor Roll' WHEN gpa >= 3.0 THEN 'Good Standing' ELSE 'Academic Probation' END AS tier FROM students) student_tiers GROUP BY tier ORDER BY student_count DESC, tier ASC;

title: Join Customers with Pre-Aggregated Spending Derived Table
description_markdown: Join `customers c` with a derived table in the FROM clause that aggregates completed order spend per customer (`(SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY customer_id) spends`). Return `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`, and `spends.total_spent`. Order by `spends.total_spent` DESC, `c.customer_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Join customer records with spending derived table
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, spends.total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY customer_id
) spends ON c.customer_id = spends.customer_id
ORDER BY spends.total_spent DESC, c.customer_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, spends.total_spent FROM customers c JOIN (SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY customer_id) spends ON c.customer_id = spends.customer_id ORDER BY spends.total_spent DESC, c.customer_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Pre-aggregates orders into a derived table before joining with customer dimensions to prevent cartesian inflation.
common_mistakes: Joining first and grouping after, which can cause severe performance degradation on large tables.
interview_tip: Pre-aggregating in derived tables before joining dimensions is a core SQL optimization design pattern.
hints: Build the derived table `spends` aggregating orders where `order_status = 'completed'`.
Join on `c.customer_id = spends.customer_id`.

Query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, spends.total_spent FROM customers c JOIN (SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY customer_id) spends ON c.customer_id = spends.customer_id ORDER BY spends.total_spent DESC, c.customer_id ASC;

title: Join Projects with Derived Assignment Workload Table
description_markdown: Join `projects p` with a derived table calculating total logged hours and staffing count per project (`(SELECT project_id, SUM(hours_worked) AS total_hours, COUNT(*) AS staff_count FROM assignments GROUP BY project_id) stats`) on `p.project_id = stats.project_id`. Return `p.project_id`, `p.project_name`, `stats.total_hours`, and `stats.staff_count`. Order by `stats.total_hours` DESC, `p.project_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Join projects with pre-aggregated workload
SELECT p.project_id, p.project_name, stats.total_hours, stats.staff_count
FROM projects p
JOIN (
  SELECT project_id, SUM(hours_worked) AS total_hours, COUNT(*) AS staff_count
  FROM assignments
  GROUP BY project_id
) stats ON p.project_id = stats.project_id
ORDER BY stats.total_hours DESC, p.project_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT p.project_id, p.project_name, stats.total_hours, stats.staff_count FROM projects p JOIN (SELECT project_id, SUM(hours_worked) AS total_hours, COUNT(*) AS staff_count FROM assignments GROUP BY project_id) stats ON p.project_id = stats.project_id ORDER BY stats.total_hours DESC, p.project_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Aggregates project assignments in a derived table and joins to project details, keeping outer logic clean.
common_mistakes: Leaving off the group by project_id in the derived subquery.
interview_tip: Pre-aggregating details tables keeps the grain of the outer query at one row per project.
hints: In the derived table: `SELECT project_id, SUM(hours_worked) AS total_hours, COUNT(*) AS staff_count FROM assignments GROUP BY project_id`.
Join on `p.project_id = stats.project_id`.

Query: SELECT p.project_id, p.project_name, stats.total_hours, stats.staff_count FROM projects p JOIN (SELECT project_id, SUM(hours_worked) AS total_hours, COUNT(*) AS staff_count FROM assignments GROUP BY project_id) stats ON p.project_id = stats.project_id ORDER BY stats.total_hours DESC, p.project_id ASC;

title: Join Faculty with Pre-Aggregated Teaching Load
description_markdown: Join `professors p` with a derived table summarizing course offerings (`(SELECT professor_id, COUNT(*) AS course_count, SUM(credits) AS total_credits FROM courses WHERE professor_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY professor_id) c_stats`) on `p.professor_id = c_stats.professor_id`. Return `p.professor_id`, `p.first_name`, `p.last_name`, `c_stats.course_count`, and `c_stats.total_credits`. Order by `c_stats.total_credits` DESC, `p.professor_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Join faculty with course credits derived table
SELECT p.professor_id, p.first_name, p.last_name, c_stats.course_count, c_stats.total_credits
FROM professors p
JOIN (
  SELECT professor_id, COUNT(*) AS course_count, SUM(credits) AS total_credits
  FROM courses
  WHERE professor_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY professor_id
) c_stats ON p.professor_id = c_stats.professor_id
ORDER BY c_stats.total_credits DESC, p.professor_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT p.professor_id, p.first_name, p.last_name, c_stats.course_count, c_stats.total_credits FROM professors p JOIN (SELECT professor_id, COUNT(*) AS course_count, SUM(credits) AS total_credits FROM courses WHERE professor_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY professor_id) c_stats ON p.professor_id = c_stats.professor_id ORDER BY c_stats.total_credits DESC, p.professor_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Pre-aggregates teaching credits in an inline derived table and joins to professors, preserving individual faculty attributes.
common_mistakes: Not excluding NULL professor_id in the derived table.
interview_tip: Derived tables prevent cartesian duplication when joining across 1-to-many relationships.
hints: Derive `c_stats` with `SELECT professor_id, COUNT(*) AS course_count, SUM(credits) AS total_credits FROM courses WHERE professor_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY professor_id`.
Join with `professors p` on `p.professor_id = c_stats.professor_id`.

Query: SELECT p.professor_id, p.first_name, p.last_name, c_stats.course_count, c_stats.total_credits FROM professors p JOIN (SELECT professor_id, COUNT(*) AS course_count, SUM(credits) AS total_credits FROM courses WHERE professor_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY professor_id) c_stats ON p.professor_id = c_stats.professor_id ORDER BY c_stats.total_credits DESC, p.professor_id ASC;

title: Double Aggregation: Average of Departmental Averages
description_markdown: Calculate the overall average of departmental average salaries using a derived table. In the inner subquery, compute `AVG(salary) AS dept_avg` grouped by `dept_id` for departments where `dept_id IS NOT NULL`. In the outer query, return `ROUND(AVG(dept_avg), 2) AS overall_dept_avg`.
starter_query:
-- Double aggregation via derived table
SELECT ROUND(AVG(dept_avg), 2) AS overall_dept_avg
FROM (
  SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY dept_id
) dept_averages;
solution_query: SELECT ROUND(AVG(dept_avg), 2) AS overall_dept_avg FROM (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS dept_avg FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) dept_averages;
solution_explanation: Directly nesting `AVG(AVG(...))` is illegal in SQL. The derived table resolves this by materializing the first-stage averages for outer aggregation.
common_mistakes: Attempting to write AVG(AVG(salary)), which causes a syntax error.
interview_tip: SQL forbids nested aggregate functions; derived tables are the fundamental solution to multi-stage aggregation.
hints: Inner query calculates `AVG(salary) AS dept_avg` grouped by `dept_id`.
Outer query takes `ROUND(AVG(dept_avg), 2) AS overall_dept_avg`.
Query: SELECT ROUND(AVG(dept_avg), 2) AS overall_dept_avg FROM (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS dept_avg FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) dept_averages;

title: Double Aggregation: Extrema of Customer Order Volumes
description_markdown: Using a derived table that counts orders per customer (`(SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) customer_orders`), compute the maximum and minimum order counts across all ordering customers. Return `MAX(order_count) AS max_orders` and `MIN(order_count) AS min_orders`.
starter_query:
-- Extrema of order counts via derived table
SELECT MAX(order_count) AS max_orders, MIN(order_count) AS min_orders
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
) customer_orders;
solution_query: SELECT MAX(order_count) AS max_orders, MIN(order_count) AS min_orders FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) customer_orders;
solution_explanation: Computes counts per customer first, then computes global MAX and MIN over those counts in the outer query.
common_mistakes: Trying to compute MAX(COUNT(*)), which is not permitted.
interview_tip: This is the classic interview question: 'Find the highest and lowest volume among customers who placed orders.'
hints: Inner query: `SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id`.
Outer query: `SELECT MAX(order_count) AS max_orders, MIN(order_count) AS min_orders FROM (...) customer_orders`.
Query: SELECT MAX(order_count) AS max_orders, MIN(order_count) AS min_orders FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) customer_orders;

title: Calculate Department Pay Spread Using Derived Table
description_markdown: From a derived table in the FROM clause that computes `dept_id`, `MAX(salary) AS max_sal`, and `MIN(salary) AS min_sal` for departments with non-null `dept_id`, calculate `dept_id`, `max_sal`, `min_sal`, and `(max_sal - min_sal) AS salary_spread`. Order by `salary_spread` DESC, `dept_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Department salary spread calculation
SELECT dept_id, max_sal, min_sal, (max_sal - min_sal) AS salary_spread
FROM (
  SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) AS max_sal, MIN(salary) AS min_sal
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY dept_id
) salary_bounds
ORDER BY salary_spread DESC, dept_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT dept_id, max_sal, min_sal, (max_sal - min_sal) AS salary_spread FROM (SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) AS max_sal, MIN(salary) AS min_sal FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) salary_bounds ORDER BY salary_spread DESC, dept_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Computes boundaries in the derived table so the outer query can cleanly subtract min from max without repeating aggregates.
common_mistakes: Recalculating MAX(salary) - MIN(salary) multiple times.
interview_tip: Derived tables prevent redundant evaluations and simplify complex computed expressions.
hints: Derive `max_sal` and `min_sal` per department in the subquery.
Subtract `(max_sal - min_sal) AS salary_spread` in the outer SELECT.

Query: SELECT dept_id, max_sal, min_sal, (max_sal - min_sal) AS salary_spread FROM (SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) AS max_sal, MIN(salary) AS min_sal FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) salary_bounds ORDER BY salary_spread DESC, dept_id ASC;

title: Filter High Margin Products via Derived Profit Table
description_markdown: From a derived table that calculates unit profit `(price - cost) AS unit_margin` for each product (`(SELECT product_id, product_name, price, cost, (price - cost) AS unit_margin FROM products) prod_margins`), filter for products where `unit_margin >= 100.00`. Return `product_id`, `product_name`, and `unit_margin`. Order by `unit_margin` DESC, `product_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Derived table for unit profit margin
SELECT product_id, product_name, unit_margin
FROM (
  SELECT product_id, product_name, price, cost, (price - cost) AS unit_margin
  FROM products
) prod_margins
WHERE unit_margin >= 100.00
ORDER BY unit_margin DESC, product_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT product_id, product_name, unit_margin FROM (SELECT product_id, product_name, price, cost, (price - cost) AS unit_margin FROM products) prod_margins WHERE unit_margin >= 100.00 ORDER BY unit_margin DESC, product_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Allows filtering by the computed `unit_margin` alias directly in the outer WHERE clause.
common_mistakes: Trying to filter by unit_margin in a WHERE clause of the inner query before it has been defined.
interview_tip: Standard SQL does not permit WHERE clause filtering on aliases defined in the same SELECT; derived tables solve this.
hints: Derive `(price - cost) AS unit_margin` in the subquery.
Filter `WHERE unit_margin >= 100.00` in the outer query.

Query: SELECT product_id, product_name, unit_margin FROM (SELECT product_id, product_name, price, cost, (price - cost) AS unit_margin FROM products) prod_margins WHERE unit_margin >= 100.00 ORDER BY unit_margin DESC, product_id ASC;

title: Filter High Final Exam Scores via Derived Table

solution_explanation: Isolates final exam scores into a virtual dataset in FROM, then applies grade cutoff criteria.

interview_tip: Pre-filtering partitions of a large table in FROM simplifies multi-step reporting pipelines.
hints: Select `enrollment_id, score` from `marks` where `assessment_type = 'final'` in the subquery.
Filter `score >= 90.00` in the outer query.

title: Order Status Breakdown via Derived Table
description_markdown: From a derived table grouping orders by status (`(SELECT order_status, COUNT(*) AS status_count, SUM(total_amount) AS status_revenue FROM orders GROUP BY order_status) status_stats`), select `order_status`, `status_count`, and `status_revenue` where `status_count >= 1`. solution_query: SELECT order_status, status_count, status_revenue FROM (SELECT order_status, COUNT(*) AS status_count, SUM(total_amount) AS status_revenue FROM orders GROUP BY order_status) status_stats WHERE status_count >= 1 ORDER BY status_count DESC, order_status ASC;
solution_explanation: Groups status metrics into a derived table and queries it like an ordinary view.

interview_tip: Derived tables act as inline temporary views scoped strictly to the executing query.
hints: Derive `status_count` and `status_revenue` per `order_status`.
Filter and sort in the outer statement.

title: Calculate Department Budget Surplus via Derived Payroll
description_markdown: Join `departments d` with a derived table calculating total department payroll (`(SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) payroll`) on `d.dept_id = payroll.dept_id`. Return `d.dept_id`, `d.dept_name`, `d.budget`, `payroll.total_payroll`, and `(d.budget - payroll.total_payroll) AS budget_surplus`. Order by `budget_surplus` DESC, `d.dept_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Join department budget with pre-computed payroll
SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget, payroll.total_payroll,
       (d.budget - payroll.total_payroll) AS budget_surplus
FROM departments d
JOIN (
  SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY dept_id
) payroll ON d.dept_id = payroll.dept_id
ORDER BY budget_surplus DESC, d.dept_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget, payroll.total_payroll, (d.budget - payroll.total_payroll) AS budget_surplus FROM departments d JOIN (SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) payroll ON d.dept_id = payroll.dept_id ORDER BY budget_surplus DESC, d.dept_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Pre-aggregates total salaries by department before joining to departments to compute budget surplus.
common_mistakes: Joining first and grouping by department columns, which risks SQL mode full-group-by errors.
interview_tip: Pre-aggregating before joining is cleaner and avoids tricky GROUP BY restrictions on dimension attributes.
hints: Derive `payroll` with `SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id`.
Calculate `(d.budget - payroll.total_payroll) AS budget_surplus`.

Query: SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget, payroll.total_payroll, (d.budget - payroll.total_payroll) AS budget_surplus FROM departments d JOIN (SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id) payroll ON d.dept_id = payroll.dept_id ORDER BY budget_surplus DESC, d.dept_id ASC;

title: Join Products with Pre-Aggregated Gross Sales
description_markdown: Join `products p` with a derived table calculating total gross sales from `order_items` (`(SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_sales FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id) sales`) on `p.product_id = sales.product_id`. Return `p.product_id`, `p.product_name`, and `sales.gross_sales`. Order by `sales.gross_sales` DESC, `p.product_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Join products with derived gross sales table
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, sales.gross_sales
FROM products p
JOIN (
  SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_sales
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY product_id

ORDER BY sales.gross_sales DESC, p.product_id ASC;

title: Calculate Project Cost Per Logged Hour via Derived Table

title: Product Sales Velocity Metrics via Derived Table Join
description_markdown: Join `products p` with a derived table calculating item sales volume and unique order count (`(SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units_sold, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_orders FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id) velocity`) on `p.product_id = velocity.product_id`. Return `p.product_id`, `p.product_name`, `p.price`, `velocity.units_sold`, and `velocity.distinct_orders`. Order by `velocity.units_sold` DESC, `velocity.distinct_orders` DESC, `p.product_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Join product catalog with sales velocity derived table
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, p.price, velocity.units_sold, velocity.distinct_orders
FROM products p
JOIN (
  SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units_sold, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_orders
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY product_id
) velocity ON p.product_id = velocity.product_id
ORDER BY velocity.units_sold DESC, velocity.distinct_orders DESC, p.product_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, p.price, velocity.units_sold, velocity.distinct_orders FROM products p JOIN (SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units_sold, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_orders FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id) velocity ON p.product_id = velocity.product_id ORDER BY velocity.units_sold DESC, velocity.distinct_orders DESC, p.product_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Pre-aggregates distinct order penetration and total quantity inside a derived table before joining to product metadata.
common_mistakes: Using COUNT(order_id) instead of COUNT(DISTINCT order_id).
interview_tip: Distinct metrics over child tables should always be calculated in derived tables or CTEs to avoid inaccurate duplicates.
